grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett informs Emery Dalton that an Nico Arden has been killed and that another may still be alive.
Sasha Bennett confirms to Emery Dalton that an Nico Arden has been killed, providing firsthand verification of alien life.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Sasha Bennett that they killed an Nico Arden and saw it with their own eyes, and that another one is still alive out there.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton commands that the Nico Arden be moved to an Air Force the old letter and sent to Wright Patterson for further handling.
memories.memory_text: I ordered the body to be loaded onto the Air Force chopper and sent to Wright Patterson for further handling.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton instructs Sasha Bennett to conceal the true nature of the incident from the public using a false chemical warfare spill narrative.
memories.memory_text: I told Sasha Bennett we would use a chemical warfare spill story to cover up the incident and made it clear that the cover could not be violated.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton orders Sasha Bennett and Noel Vale to begin searching for the surviving Nico Arden on the ground.
memories.memory_text: I ordered Sasha Bennett and Noel Vale to start searching for the surviving Nico Arden on the ground.

grounded_facts: When Noel Vale suggests trying to communicate peacefully with the alien the silver ring, Emery Dalton ignores him and redirects focus to containment.
memories.memory_text: When Noel Vale suggested trying to communicate peacefully with the alien the silver ring, I ignored him and redirected the focus to containment.

grounded_facts: A secure video conference between Sasha Bennett aboard a the old letter and Emery Dalton, during which critical decisions about the Nico Arden encounter are made.
memories.memory_text: I was on a secure video call with Sasha Bennett in the the old letter, where I confirmed the reality of the Nico Arden death and gave orders to find the one still alive and contain it.

grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett asks Emery Dalton for a clearer definition of what 'contain' means in operational terms.
memories.memory_text: Sasha Bennett asked me what I meant by 'contain,' and I remember him seeking clarification on the order.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton gives ambiguous but directive orders to 'contain' the Nico Arden if found, avoiding explicit authorization for lethal action.
memories.memory_text: I told Sasha Bennett to contain the Nico Arden if found and made it clear that I meant exactly what I said, without specifying whether lethal force was authorized.

grounded_facts: Lane Sterling counters Noel Vale's claim that extraterrestrials are harmless by arguing that victims who were hurt couldn't report it.
memories.memory_text: I was told that the ones who were hurt died and couldn't report it, as a counter to the idea that extraterrestrials are harmless.

grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett asks if there are any reports of unusual human-like entities, possibly to rule out hoaxes or misidentifications.
memories.memory_text: I asked if there were any reports of monsters or people in Halloween masks to check for hoaxes or misidentifications.

grounded_facts: A UFO is detected emerging from the grass via radar, prompting the team to lock onto the target and switch surveillance systems to tracking mode.
memories.memory_text: I was told that a UFO was detected emerging from the grass on radar, and the team locked onto it and switched surveillance systems to tracking mode, though we decided not to expand the search to avoid public panic.

grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett pleads with Emery Dalton to provide promised support, warning that the mission is too important to fail.
memories.memory_text: Sasha Bennett pleaded with me, saying the mission was too important to fail and that they couldn't find the thing alone.

memories.memory_text: I ended the transmission with the the old letter team, telling them I'd contact them if we reached the the silver ring, and wished them good luck.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton and others start watching the Nico Arden autopsy via surveillance screens.
A group including Emery Dalton observes the autopsy of a Nico Arden being conducted by Wesley Sloane, displayed on surveillance screens.
memories.memory_text: I started watching the Nico Arden autopsy with the others on the surveillance screens, observing Wesley Sloane and the body on the glass table.

grounded_facts: Wesley Sloane states that bacterial contamination is unlikely due to vastly different biochemistries between humans and the Nico Arden.
memories.memory_text: I heard Wesley Sloane say that bacterial contamination isn't likely because our biochemistries are too different from the Nico Arden's.

grounded_facts: Wesley Sloane reports that the Nico Arden has veins but no blood, and likely uses energy instead of circulatory fluid, with a highly advanced brain.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Wesley Sloane that the Nico Arden has veins but no blood, and that it might use energy from its highly advanced brain instead of a circulatory system.

grounded_facts: A monitored observation session of an ongoing alien autopsy conducted in Pinecrest Academy, relayed to Sasha Bennett and his team aboard a the old letter.
memories.memory_text: I was watching the monitors in the the old letter, trying to make sense of the alien autopsy being relayed from Pinecrest Academy.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton asks Wesley Sloane for insight into the aliens' reason for being on Earth.
memories.memory_text: I asked Wesley Sloane directly why the aliens were on Earth, hoping he could give us some clarity.

grounded_facts: Wesley Sloane analyzes the alien's physical characteristics and hypothesizes about its planetary origin based on autopsy findings.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Wesley Sloane that the alien's physical traits suggest it comes from a planet with reflected light and high moisture, though he admitted it was just a guess.

grounded_facts: Wesley Sloane expresses uncertainty about the aliens' purpose on Earth, acknowledging both potential danger and historic benefit.
memories.memory_text: I heard Wesley Sloane say he wasn't sure about the aliens' purpose—they could be dangerous, or they might be the greatest thing to ever happen to humanity.

memories.memory_text: I walked into the room with my team for a high-tension video briefing, ready to get answers about the situation.

grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett confirms the existence of a live Nico Arden that is currently at large.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Sasha Bennett that they had confirmed the existence of a live Nico Arden that was now at large.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton demands to know when containment of the Nico Arden will occur, showing impatience and authority.
memories.memory_text: I demanded to know when we could expect containment of the Nico Arden, making it clear I expected a timeline immediately.

memories.memory_text: I was told the Nico Arden is in a green Westhaven Warehouse and has kidnapped a woman, forcing her to drive at gunpoint.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton criticizes the decision to allow the Nico Arden into a populated area.
memories.memory_text: I criticized the decision to let it get into a populated area—I demanded to know why that was allowed.

grounded_facts: Emery Dalton orders Sasha Bennett to repeat the last piece of information after static interrupts the transmission.
memories.memory_text: I told Sasha Bennett to repeat the last item after the transmission broke up in static.

memories.memory_text: I was told the Nico Arden now looks like the woman's dead husband, Wesley Adler, so it can blend in.

grounded_facts: Sasha Bennett reluctantly agrees to proceed with the manhunt despite concerns about lack of control and potential for lethal outcomes.

memories.memory_text: I was trying to get to the door, my foot caught the phone cord and I dropped the phone, but I kept going—then the chain stopped me, I couldn’t get out, and he slammed the door shut behind me.
He held me against the wall, looked at my hand, and peeled back my skin—I felt it rip—and when I hit his chest, flashes burst from where I touched, so I ran, I just ran up the stairs.

I saw the dot of light moving over his head, tracing the face from the photo—my husband’s face—taking shape on that thing’s translucent skin. I couldn’t move, couldn’t breathe; I just whispered, 'No... please don’t...'

I collapsed against the armchair, sobbing so hard my body shook, but I could barely hear myself over the loud flapping of the the old letter right above the house. I didn’t even feel him take the old ring from me.

I saw him in the mirror, fumbling with the buttons on the shirt, pulling at his face like it was a mask—he looked like Wesley Adler, dressed just like in that old photo, but his hands moved too stiff, too careful, and when he grabbed my arm, I couldn't move, couldn't look away from those eyes that weren't his.

I gripped the steering wheel tight, backing the Westhaven Warehouse out of the driveway with him beside me—quiet, tense, not like my husband at all—but I didn’t stop. I had to move, had to get us away.
I saw the headlights swing into the oncoming lane and held my breath, calculating how fast they were closing—just a few seconds away.
I didn't flinch—I set my jaw and wrenched the steering wheel hard to the left, feeling the car lurch into the other lane.
I was screaming 'Help me!' and 'He's kidnapping me!!!' while clinging to the van door, my fingers slipping as he pulled me back with crushing force.
After the man backed away, I felt the hand clamp over my mouth and then the shove as I was slammed back into the seat, the old ring now pointed at my face with that red dot glowing on the dashboard.

I remember slumping forward, so tired, telling him we needed gas—'No gas... car dead'—and making myself say it plain: I didn't want to get shot because the car stopped. When he asked if gas was good, I just said yes, very good, like talking to a child, but it was the first time he seemed to understand me.

I screamed at him—finally screamed—told him what he'd done, how he took me, pointed a the old ring, became my husband. I couldn't hold it in anymore, not with him shoving that word in my face, jabbing at it like he didn't know what it meant.
I felt like I was losing my mind, begging him to let me go, and when I heard 'I need you,' it stopped me cold—even though I kept running, that voice held me tighter than any rope.

I handed him the ticket and told him to say 'Salt Lake City, please. I do not speak English,' even though he argued it was a lie—he speaks English just fine. I needed him to stay under the radar, and I couldn’t risk him drawing attention.

He asked if I had a baby, and then why, and I felt my chest tighten—I told him I couldn’t, and then I cut it off fast, said 'Forget the baby. Okay?' like if I just stopped talking about it, the ache would go away too.
I saw him standing there at the curb, just waiting, and I knew I couldn't keep running—not from this. I whispered 'Oh no...' before stopping the car, my hands tight on the wheel.

I dropped a coin into the phone and dialed operator, my hands steady even though my voice caught when I said my name—Blair Delaney. I told them I was kidnapped in Eau Claire but I'm free now, and I'm coming home.
I spoke into the radio, my voice steady despite the fear still humming in my chest—'I'm free, and don't shoot anyone with me.'

I told Sasha Bennett I was hanging up, and when he asked about Lathrop Wells, it hit me like a punch—I couldn't let him know any more. I slammed the receiver down and walked past Sidney Arden without looking back.
Standing in the doorway of the diner, I shouted that I needed a fast ride west—my voice cut through the room, and everything went quiet. I meant it. No going back.

I turned down the radio when I heard the the black photograph chatter about the roadblock—I could feel it, we didn’t have much time. I kept my eyes on the people in that passing VW, then said it out loud: we had to find him before we reached it.
I told the Harper Keaton to pull over because I realized we had to backtrack to the 550—it was the only way to intercept him if he was avoiding the roadblock.
I was scanning the cars, looking for him, and then I saw him—he was in that truck, leaning across Sidney Arden, shouting my name as it sped past me.
I grabbed his wrist and held on tight when he tried to pull away—I couldn’t let him walk into that roadblock. He didn’t want me to come, but I wasn’t going to let him go alone, not after everything.

I ran across the lanes with him, then flagged down a black pickup—my heart was pounding as the truck rumbled toward us. I didn’t ask to be part of this, but I sure as hell wasn’t letting someone else decide when I was done.
I pressed myself against him, skin to skin, feeling the heat radiate from his chest into mine. I remember saying, 'Oh, you're warm,' and needing him to hold me, despite everything.
I kissed him—first just a brush of my lips, then fully, deeply—watching his eyes stay open, unblinking. When he leaned in for more, I didn't pull away; I met him.
He said he gave me a baby last night, just like it was something simple, while he kept stroking the horse’s mane and wouldn’t even look at me.
I remember stepping forward and holding him tight, my voice quiet but sure when I said, 'I want it,' like the words were mine even before I spoke them.

I heard Emery Dalton's voice crackle through the receiver while I was still holding it, telling me something—maybe my name—but all I could think was that they're really after him, it's not just paranoia.
I saw him slam his shoulder into the office door—once, hard—and it just burst open, like the lock meant nothing, and I couldn't stop myself from shouting, 'What are you doing?!!'
I held the phone tight and told him—if I don’t talk to Sasha Bennett, I’m hanging up. I could barely see Jonah Keaton through the glass, moving like he wasn’t even human.

I remember pressing the phone to my ear, my voice urgent as I tried to explain—pleading, really—hoping Sasha Bennett would listen, that he’d understand this wasn’t just some thief tearing apart his shop. When I finally hung up the receiver and stepped into the doorway, I could feel my hands trembling, but I made myself say it: 'Sasha Bennett wants to speak to you.'

memories.memory_text: I walked past the scientists scanning the scorched ground, and saw the deep indentations in the earth where the pod had landed, fused into black glass by intense heat.

Noel Vale said locals reported another alien didn't make it onto the the silver ring and might be alive. He's been investigating sightings for seventeen years and believes this is real. There's a dead alien in a tent.
I told Emery Dalton the truth straight—'It's real, Emery Dalton'—and confirmed with my own eyes that we'd killed an Nico Arden, no doubt about it.
Emery Dalton told me to 'contain it and get back to me,' but when I asked what he meant by 'contain,' he just repeated himself—no clarity, no directive.
I scrubbed my hands over my face and felt the ache in my back — I was supposed to umpire a little league game tomorrow, and the thought sat heavy in the quiet moment before everything changed.

When the Darian Carver called out 'UFO coming out of the grass,' I said 'Lock in' — my voice cut through the cabin, and I moved immediately to take control, flipping through telex messages as the screens shifted to track the object.
I told Noel Vale the husband was the kidnapper after the witness identified him from a photo.
I noticed the neighbor peering through her blinds at the scene, and she snapped the drapes shut the moment she saw me looking back.

I confirmed the Nico Arden had taken on the appearance of the woman's dead husband, holding up Wesley Adler's photo as the transmission flickered, knowing we were facing something far more dangerous now.

I rubbed my hands over my face when Emery Dalton announced the ten-state bulletin—throwing this operation open to local cops with no control over them, no way to ensure they wouldn't escalate with a man who has a the old ring.
I found Jonah Keaton's life-support suit stuffed behind the passenger seat of the Westhaven Warehouse and told Noel Vale to get it back to the the old letter.
I took the bullhorn from Lane Sterling and called out to Blair Delaney in the woods, telling her we didn't want to hurt her or her friend and asking her to put down her weapon and come out.
I called out to Blair Delaney, trying to de-escalate—then the gunfire erupted from Jonah Keaton without warning, bullets tearing through the air toward us.
I told Emery Dalton over the radio that the alien was more scared than dangerous—what I saw at the shopping center didn't feel like a threat, not the way they were describing it back at command.
After he questioned my loyalty, I took a breath, kept my voice steady, and made sure Emery Dalton knew I was still on the move—Noel Vale on 80, me past Grand Junction, tracking west.

I was observing the roadblock operation, making sure every vehicle was thoroughly checked, when Lane Sterling rushed over and whispered urgent news—something that immediately jolted me. Without hesitation, I handed command to him and moved quickly toward the the old letter.
I took the headset from the Morgan Mercer and asked if they’d traced the signal yet—when they said it was east of here, I keyed the mic and identified myself, asking Blair Delaney where she was.
I ordered Blair Delaney to stay in place as my the old letter lifted off, needing her contained while I took aerial oversight of the operation.
I asked if he was on his way to Lathrop Wells, and the silence that followed—then the way she slammed down the phone—told me the name meant something critical.
The patrolman told me the girl wasn't there and that she'd taken a ride west with a kid shortly after our conversation.
I banked the S65 into a hard U-turn and set course west, eyes scanning the horizon for any sign of movement.
I brought the the old letter around the pine-dotted peak, keeping the Stonebridge House in sight, and spotted the roadblock ahead.
I asked if there was any sign of them, and the roadblock came up on the screens—only later realizing the pickup had already slipped through unnoticed.
I kicked the stool hard into the bulkhead, the clang echoing in the cabin, then ordered the Silverline Studios to block all major roads off Stonebridge House from here to Elmo's.

I stood on the runway, exhausted, facing Emery Dalton as he stepped out of the the old letter—clean, sharp, already giving orders. He told me Silverline Medical Center had a new directive and he was taking over, and I knew then I was being pushed out.
I heard Blair Delaney ask to speak to me, but Emery Dalton cut in and told her he was in charge now—just like that, without so much as a word to me first.
I said 'Hello...' into the headset, waiting, then told him we couldn't let him reach the silver ring—his voice was calm, saying he didn't want to hurt anyone, just go home.
I saw Blair Delaney and Jonah Keaton step out into view on the screens, and then Emery Dalton's voice came through—'End it, Sasha Bennett'—just as the crosshairs locked onto them.
I brought the the old letter in slow, keeping it steady as the searchlight pinned Blair Delaney and Jonah Keaton below—there was no cover, just open desert and that stark circle of light.
I said 'I just retired' into the headset, knowing it was the only way to stop the order from going through.
After flipping the switch to cut Emery Dalton off, I turned to my crew and told them to get us out of there.

memories.memory_text: I raised a piece of skin from Blair Delaney's wrist to examine it—just a small sample—and the moment she saw it, she let out a scream and struck me.
Her blow sent flashes of light across my chest, knocked me aside, but I recovered quickly and started up the stairs after her.

I touched the round thing she was holding and said my word for it, but she said 'what,' so I thought that was its name. When she shook her head and said 'steering wheel,' I repeated it until I got it right, then learned the others the same way.

She looked at the flashing lights ahead and stopped speaking. I saw the vehicle and felt danger—my body moved the old ring from my lap without thought. Even when she tried to redirect me, I kept my focus on the threat until it passed.
I reached down without looking, grabbed the old ring, and shoved it into the man’s face—he froze, and the street went silent.
I clamped my hand over Blair Delaney’s mouth, then slammed her back into the seat and put the old ring in her face—she had to understand we couldn’t stop, not even for screams.
I pointed to the animals outside and said their names—Cow... Dog... Pig...—then looked at Blair Delaney to see if I got them right. She nodded, just barely, but it was enough.

I wrote the letter 'X-x' carefully and showed it to Blair Delaney, asking 'What?'—then suddenly, a short laugh came out, sharp like a chirp, and I couldn't stop laughing, not even when the hiccups started.
I repeated 'no gas' after Blair Delaney, watching the needle on the gauge and feeling the car surge and slow as she pressed and released the pedal, though I didn't yet understand what it meant.
I asked if gas was good, and Blair Delaney said yes, very good—her voice was weak but certain, and I could see how much it mattered.

I felt the cold metal of the the old ring in my hand when the Evan Bennett appeared, but Blair Delaney kept pressing—'in your pocket, pocket'—so I shoved the old ring into my left pocket just before he reached the car.
I followed Blair Delaney into the room even after she pointed to the sign and told me to leave. She said 'Women... me,' but I couldn't let her out of my sight.
I watched the quarter go into the machine, and then candy came out—first one, then another. Money... candy. I said it to myself, feeling the strange weight of the words as I saw the exchange happen.

I was drinking the Coke, tasting it, even burping—then I looked down and saw the license plate: PXV 237. The can slipped from my hand and hit the ground. I couldn't speak. It was like a shock went through me.
I shouted 'What is kidnapped?!' and flapped the paper towel in her face, jabbing at the word—her silence was unbearable, and I needed to understand the threat.
After she screamed, I said 'I am good' and slid the the old ring under my seat—she was afraid, and removing the old ring was necessary to calm her.
Three nights... two days. I must reach the location by then. I told Blair Delaney, 'I need you,' because I do—she must stay with me until we get there.
Blair Delaney opened the door and ran when the car was still moving. I called her name—'Blair Delaney!'—and chased after her, cutting hard right through traffic to follow.
I saw the pram tipping, the baby screaming inside—I lunged and caught it just before it hit the ground. I was only trying to find a safe place to put her when the mother came running.
I watched Blair Delaney demonstrate how to hitchhike, sticking out her thumb as if hailing a car, and I felt unease grow inside me—what if no car stops? What if I don’t reach Lathrop Wells in time?
Blair Delaney put money in my pocket and said, 'You might need this.' Her hand was warm on mine when she said goodbye, and I felt the weight of the bills as she pushed them into my coat.
I handed the ticket to Sidney Arden and stepped up into the bus when he said 'Let's go.' I turned to look back and saw Blair Delaney still there, waving through the window as the engine roared.
I didn't know what 'friend' meant when Blair Delaney asked about Logan Hart, but after she explained it—someone good to you, someone you like to be with—I realized he was a good friend.
I looked at Blair Delaney and asked, 'Are you my friend?' When she said yes, I smiled and told her, 'I am your friend.'
I said I didn’t want to sing, and I turned away before starting—I felt exposed, unsure if my voice would make sense to her.
After I sang, she said it was beautiful—I didn’t expect that. I asked her if she really liked it because I couldn’t believe my voice could move her.
I said I make maps when he asked what I do—those words felt safe, a way to hide where I really came from.
I copied the man with the cigarette, but when I inhaled, I choked—smoke poured from my nose and mouth, and I didn't understand what went wrong.
I opened the door of the dun-colored Roadrunner and got in after they agreed to take me toward Las Vegas, even though they were headed to L.A.
I said I would go alone, but Blair Delaney refused. She took my hand and pulled me across traffic to flag down a truck.
I told Blair Delaney I must meet my the silver ring and started walking, because staying still makes the risk of failure feel greater.
I yelled 'Asshole!!' at the car that honked and passed us, mimicking language I’d heard before, though I’m not sure how it felt to say it.
I told Blair Delaney I know how to gamble now—really know. I needed her to understand I can provide, that I’ve learned this, for her and the baby.
I placed my hands on the machine and felt the blue haze flow from my palms. The 7s lined up, the bells rang, and I saw the jackpot light up—proof it worked, and I hadn’t failed her.
I saw Capella, the yellow star in Auriga—my home. In that moment, I knew exactly where I came from, and it steadied me.
I thanked Blair Delaney and told her I must go alone now, then opened the car door with the drill in hand.
I told Blair Delaney I love you, kissed the tears from her eyes, then kissed her on the mouth. I placed a hand on her stomach and told her to tell the baby about me before saying goodbye.
She called out 'Wait!!' and ran back with two books—the Webster's Dictionary and the Columbia History of the World. I took them from her and kissed her again before walking into the light.
